newsitem.title: USA: The major players in the Oklahoma bombing trial.
newsitem.headline: The major players in the Oklahoma bombing trial.

text.p: Following are the major players in the Oklahoma City bombing trial that begins with jury selection on March 31.

-- Timothy McVeigh, 28 and a Gulf War veteran, is charged in the bombing with former Army buddy Terry Nichols. The two will be tried separately. Prosecutors say they turned against the government during the 1993 standoff between the FBI and the Branch Davidian sect in Waco, Texas. McVeigh left the Army in late 1991 and returned to his native western New York where he worked as a security guard in Buffalo. In 1993 he became a drifter, working odd jobs and selling guns. The tall, lanky McVeigh is considered bright. He has appeared animated during pre-trial hearings, much to the chagrin of bombing victims.

-- U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch, 66, was appointed in 1974 by President Richard Nixon. Matsch generally is respected by prosecutors and defence attorneys, although they incur his sharp rebukes as he maintains iron-handed control of his courtroom.

In 1987, he sentenced two white supremacists to 150 years each in prison in the murder of Denver radio talk show host Alan Berg, a Jew. He was assigned to the bombing case after an appeals court disqualified an Oklahoma City judge. Matsch ruled the defendants could not get a fair trial in Oklahoma and moved the case to Denver. He was born in Burlington, Iowa.
He is expected to keep the pace of the trial moving along.

-- The lead prosecutor representing the government is Joseph Hartzler, 46, who has spent all but four years of his legal career as a Justice Department attorney. He obtained convictions in Chicago of four terrorists who sought independence for Puerto Rico for seditious conspiracy, and of a county judge in a corruption case.

Hartzler was picked by Attorney General Janet Reno to oversee the bombing case. He graduated first in his law school class at American University. He was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 1989 and uses a motorized scooter. He was born in Columbus, Ohio.

-- McVeigh's lead attorney, Stephen Jones has represented other unpopular defendants and causes in his 31 years of practicing law, handling 25 death-penalty cases and a lawsuit against substandard prisons. He served four years as general counsel of the American Civil Liberties Union Oklahoma affiliate. He also has been a prosecutor. A Republican, he ran unsuccessfully for the U.S. Senate and for attorney general of Oklahoma, his adopted state.
The 56-year-old attorney was born in Lafayette, La.

-- Michael Fortier, 28, will be a key witness for the prosecution. He was a friend of McVeigh's from the army and lived in Kingman, Ariz. Fortier has pleaded guilty to four felony accounts in return for testifying that he knew about plans for the bombing, but did nothing to stop it. He is expected to testify that he and McVeigh drove to Oklahoma City where McVeigh told him the Alfed P. Murrah federal building was the target. He faces up to 23 years in prison.

-- Lori Fortier, Michael Fortier's wife, is also expected to testify for the prosecution. Her husband's agreement to testify in exchange for a lesser charge also allowed her to escape prosecution. She is expected to testify about a phony South Dakota driver's license that McVeigh allegedly made for himself bearing the name Robert Kling, an alias the government says McVeigh used.
